Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, an initial vector $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, a finite or infinite sequence of finite gradient vectors $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, positive step sizes $\eta_t>0$, a decay parameter $\rho\in[0,1)$, and a denominator constant $\epsilon>0$. $$r_{t,i}=\rho r_{t-1,i}+(1-\rho)g_{t,i}^2\qquad(1\le i\le d),$$

and then set

$$x_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\eta_t\frac{g_{t,i}}{\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon}\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$

For a finite gradient sequence of length $T\ge0$, perform rounds $1\le t\le T$ and return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$; when $T=0$, return $(x_1)$. For an infinite gradient sequence, perform every round $t\ge1$, thereby defining and returning the iterate sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge1}$. The root, addition, and division in the update are coordinatewise. The procedure makes no convergence or regret claim.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge1$, an initial scalar $x_1\in[-1,1]$, a step parameter $\alpha>0$, moment parameters $\beta_1\in[0,1)$ and $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, a denominator parameter $\epsilon\ge0$, and a sequence of scalar gradients $g_1,\ldots,g_T$. Set $m_0=v_0=0$. At round $t$, update

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2.$$

The input is admissible only when $v_t+\epsilon>0$ at every update. Set $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$, compute $y_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t m_t/\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$, and set $x_{t+1}=\max(-1,\min(1,y_{t+1}))$. Thus the iterate is projected onto $[-1,1]$ after the update. Return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$, whose final iterate is $x_{T+1}$. The denominator parameter is added inside the square root. No moment bias correction is applied.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, a finite horizon $T\ge1$, a nonempty compact convex set $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an initial point $x_1\in F$, positive step sizes $\alpha_t>0$, a fixed parameter $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, and parameters $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$ for $1\le t\le T$. $$\widehat v_{t,i}=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1,i},v_{t,i}\}.$$

At a successor round, each recurrence is a finite sum of products of finite reals by [F1]–[F3] and [F9]; the coefficients $\rho,1-\rho,\beta_2,1-\beta_2$ are nonnegative, and each squared gradient is nonnegative by [F5], so the next second moment remains nonnegative.

For RMSProp, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}\ge0$, so $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon>0$ by [F1]. For Adam, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$ because $v_t\ge0$ and $\epsilon\ge0$; its positivity is the explicit admissibility condition in [F2]. Thus each stated quotient has a positive denominator.

In AMSGrad, both entries in each maximum are finite and nonnegative by [F3], [F5], and step 1.1. The maximum exists by [F7] and is nonnegative. If $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, then $\widehat v_{t-1,i}=v_{t,i}=0$. Since $\beta_2>0$, $1-\beta_2>0$, and both summands defining $v_{t,i}$ are nonnegative, $v_{t-1,i}=0$ and $g_{t,i}=0$. Repeating this argument back to time zero gives every earlier $g_{s,i}=0$; the first-moment recurrence then gives $m_{t,i}=m_{t-1,i}=0$. Conversely, if $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, some $v_{s,i}>0$ for $s\le t$, and then $v_{u+1,i}\ge\beta_2v_{u,i}>0$ for each $u\ge s$, so $v_{t,i}>0$. The zero-ratio convention in [F3] is therefore consistent with the recurrence.

Fix a round and its finite vector $y$ and nonnegative weights $q_i=\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$. Since $F$ is compact, [F8] bounds $\|x\|_2$ by some $B$ for $x\in F$. For $x,z\in F$, coordinatewise expansion and [F9] give $$\left|\sum_i q_i(x_i-y_i)^2-\sum_i q_i(z_i-y_i)^2\right|\le\|x-z\|_2\sum_i q_i(2B+2\|y\|_2).$$ Thus the objective is continuous on $F$. (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with The reals form a totally ordered field,
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).

Induction gives $0\le a_{t,j}\le\beta_1^{t-j}$: the terminal coefficient is at most $1$, and each earlier coefficient acquires one factor at most $\beta_1$.

By [F3] applied to $\sqrt{a_{t,j}}$ and $\sqrt{a_{t,j}}g_{j,i}$, $$m_{t,i}^2\le\left(\sum_{j=1}^ta_{t,j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^ta_{t,j}g_{j,i}^2\right) \le\frac{1}{1-\beta_1}\sum_{j=1}^t\beta_1^{t-j}g_{j,i}^2,$$ because $\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\beta_1^k=(1-\beta_1^t)/(1-\beta_1)\le1/(1-\beta_1)$. Iterating the second-moment recurrence [F1] gives $v_{t,i}=(1-\beta_2)\sum_{j=1}^t\beta_2^{t-j}g_{j,i}^2$. By [F2] and [F5], $\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}\ge\sqrt{v_{t,i}}$. If this value is zero, [F2] makes the energy term zero. Otherwise, for each nonzero $g_{j,i}$, $$\sqrt{v_{t,i}}\ge\sqrt{1-\beta_2}\,\sqrt{\beta_2^{t-j}}|g_{j,i}|.$$ The root recursion gives $\sqrt{\beta_2^n}=(\sqrt{\beta_2})^n$ for every integer $n\ge0$; induction proves this because both sides are nonnegative and have the same square. Also $\beta_1^n/(\sqrt{\beta_2})^n=(\beta_1/\sqrt{\beta_2})^n$ by the integer-power recursion, so $\beta_1^n/\sqrt{\beta_2^n}=\gamma^n$. Using step 2.1 termwise in the finite sum therefore gives $$\frac{m_{t,i}^2}{\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}} \le\frac{1}{(1-\beta_1)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}}\sum_{j=1}^t\gamma^{t-j}|g_{j,i}|.$$ Zero gradient terms contribute zero.

Multiply step 3.1 by $\alpha/\sqrt t$, sum over $t$ and coordinates, and reorder the finite sums. Since $1/\sqrt t\le1/\sqrt j$ for $t\ge j$ and $(1-\gamma)\sum_{k=0}^{T-j}\gamma^k=1-\gamma^{T-j+1}\le1$ by the same finite telescoping identity from step 2.1, $$\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\sum_i\frac{m_{t,i}^2}{\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}} \le\frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} \sum_i\sum_{j=1}^T|g_{j,i}|\sum_{t=j}^T\frac{\gamma^{t-j}}{\sqrt t} \le\frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)(1-\gamma)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}}\sum_i\sum_{j=1}^T\frac{|g_{j,i}|}{\sqrt j}.$$ This is the stated inequality.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge1$, an initial scalar $x_1\in[-1,1]$, a step parameter $\alpha>0$, moment parameters $\beta_1\in[0,1)$ and $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, a denominator parameter $\epsilon\ge0$, and a sequence of scalar gradients $g_1,\ldots,g_T$. Set $m_0=v_0=0$. At round $t$, update

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2.$$

The input is admissible only when $v_t+\epsilon>0$ at every update. Set $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$, compute $y_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t m_t/\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$, and set $x_{t+1}=\max(-1,\min(1,y_{t+1}))$. Thus the iterate is projected onto $[-1,1]$ after the update. Return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$, whose final iterate is $x_{T+1}$. The denominator parameter is added inside the square root. No moment bias correction is applied.

For every finite admissible run of the RMSProp, uncorrected Adam, or uncorrected AMSGrad procedures defined on this page, all moment coordinates are finite and all second-moment coordinates are nonnegative. Every denominator specified by the procedure is positive. For AMSGrad, a zero historical-maximum coordinate has zero current and previous first moments, and the raw second moment is positive whenever its historical maximum is positive; the zero-ratio convention is therefore consistent. Each weighted minimization over the compact feasible set attains a minimum.
For every real $q\in[0,1)$, every $p\in\{1,2\}$, and every real $\delta>0$, there is an integer $N\ge1$ such that $n^p q^n<\delta$ for every integer $n\ge N$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $x_0\in[-1,1]$, and let $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$. Let real increments $\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n$ satisfy $\delta_j\le0$ for $j\le k$ and $\delta_j\ge0$ for $j>k$. Define $c(y)=\max\{-1,\min\{1,y\}\}$ and $x_j=c(x_{j-1}+\delta_j)$. Then

$$x_n\ge\min\left\{1,x_0+\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_j\right\}.$$

Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. $$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$

$\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers with its order (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),

A **sequence of reals** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$. We write
$x_k$ for the value $x(k)$, call it the **$k$-th term**, and write $(x_k)$, or

- $(x_k)$ is **bounded** if there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that Conventions: $\sup \emptyset$, unbounded sets, and the extended reals records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order (Ordered field). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving (Ordered field); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, a finite horizon $T\ge1$, a nonempty compact convex set $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an initial point $x_1\in F$, positive step sizes $\alpha_t>0$, a fixed parameter $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, and parameters $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$ for $1\le t\le T$. Use one-based coordinate notation $z_i:=z(i-1)$ for every vector $z\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le i\le d$. At round $t$, receive a finite subgradient vector $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$. Set $m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0$ and update coordinatewise by

$$m_{t,i}=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_{t,i},\qquad v_{t,i}=\beta_2v_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_2)g_{t,i}^2,$$

$$\widehat v_{t,i}=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1,i},v_{t,i}\}.$$

If $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\alpha_t m_{t,i}/\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$; if $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}$. Choose any minimizer

$$x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}(x_i-y_{t+1,i})^2.$$

Return the trajectory through $x_{T+1}$. The procedure uses the uncorrected first and second moments and the coordinatewise running maximum of the raw second moment. It contains no denominator stabilizer.

Let $d,T\in\mathbb N$ with $d,T\ge1$. Let $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and convex, choose $x_1\in F$, and suppose a finite $D_\infty\ge0$ satisfies $|x_i-u_i|\le D_\infty$ for every $x,u\in F$ and coordinate $i$. Let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_T:F\to\mathbb R$ be continuous convex losses, choose $g_t\in\partial\ell_t(x_t)$, and assume $|g_{t,i}|\le G_\infty$ for all $t,i$, where $G_\infty\ge0$. Run uncorrected AMSGrad with $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$ for $\alpha>0$, fixed $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, $\beta_1=\beta_{1,1}\in[0,1)$, $0\le\beta_{1,t}\le\beta_1$, and $\gamma=\beta_1/\sqrt{\beta_2}<1$. For a comparator $u\in F$, define $R_T(u)=\sum_{t=1}^T(\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u))$; the best-comparator regret is $R_T=\sup_{u\in F}R_T(u)$. Then
$$R_T(u)\le \frac{D_\infty^2\sqrt T}{2\alpha(1-\beta_1)}\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{\widehat v_{T,i}} +\frac{D_\infty^2}{(1-\beta_1)^2}\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{\beta_{1,t}\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}}{\alpha_t} +\frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)^2(1-\gamma)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} \sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{|g_{t,i}|}{\sqrt t}.$$
If, in addition, $\beta_{1,t}=\beta_1\lambda^{t-1}$ for a fixed $\lambda\in[0,1)$ or $\beta_{1,t}=\beta_1/t$, then with the other displayed parameters fixed, the best-comparator regret satisfies $R_T=O(\sqrt T)$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex (A convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ contains every line segment between two of its points). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length.

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
(Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set, the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed (Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set).

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length, Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space)
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (Convex and strictly convex functions on Euclidean convex sets), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Every complete ordered field $F$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
(Ordered field). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ (Field) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) with its order
(Order on the reals).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that Conventions: $\sup \emptyset$, unbounded sets, and the extended reals records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order (Ordered field). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving (Ordered field); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: The interval $[-1,1]$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded by [F9], hence compact by [F5]. For $x,y\in[-1,1]$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, [F8] gives $-1\le(1-\theta)x+\theta y\le1$, so the domain is convex. Also $\ell_t((1-\theta)x+\theta y)=(1-\theta)\ell_t(x)+\theta\ell_t(y)$, so each loss is convex by [F3]. Since $|\ell_t(x)-\ell_t(y)|=|x-y|$, choosing $\delta=\eta$ in [F4] proves continuity for every tolerance $\eta>0$. The gradient $g_t=1$ is a subgradient because $\ell_t(y)=\ell_t(x)+(y-x)$ by [F6], and $\gamma=\beta_1/\sqrt{\beta_2}=\sqrt2/4<1$. Thus the hypotheses for [F2] hold. Iterating [F1] gives $v_t=1-2^{-t}$, which is nondecreasing, so $\widehat v_t=v_t\ge1/2$ for every $t\ge1$.

Here $\alpha_t=1/\sqrt t$ and $\beta_{1,t}=1/4$. The second term in [F2] is therefore at least $$\frac{4}{(3/4)^2}\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}\sqrt t=\frac{16}{9\sqrt2}\sum_{t=1}^T\sqrt t.$$ For $T\ge2$, at least $T/2$ indices satisfy $t\ge T/2$, so $\sum_{t=1}^T\sqrt t\ge T^{3/2}/(2\sqrt2)$. The correction term is at least $4T^{3/2}/9$.

The constant schedule is neither $\beta_{1,t}=\beta_1\lambda^{t-1}$ with $\lambda<1$ nor $\beta_{1,t}=\beta_1/t$. Since the theorem's upper-bound expression contains this positive term, that expression cannot be $O(\sqrt T)$ for this schedule: dividing its lower bound by $\sqrt T$ gives $4T/9$, which is unbounded by [F7]. The computation concerns the stated bound only and gives no lower bound on actual regret.
